tip: 여행하다 (yeohaenghada = travel) takes a direct object: 한국을 여행했어요 (hangugeul yeohaenghaesseoyo) = 'I traveled Korea' – no 'around' or 'in' needed.
사진을 찍다 (sajineul jjikda = to take a photo) – the same 찍다 you use for tapping a transit card.
한테 (hante) marks a person on the receiving end: 가족한테 보냈어요 (gajokhante bonaesseoyo = sent to my family). Places take 에 (e) instead.
못 (mot = can't) goes right before the verb: 못 잊어요 (mot ijeoyo = can't forget). It marks inability – 안 (an) would mean you simply don't.
여행을 가다 (yeohaengeul gada = to go on a trip) – trips are 'gone' in Korean, not 'made'.
랑 (rang) is the casual spoken 'with': 친구랑 (chingurang = with a friend). In formal writing you usually see 와/과 (wa/gwa) instead – same job, more formal.
예약 (yeyak) reserves places; 예매 (yemae) books tickets.
Korean splits 'wear' by body part: 입다 (ipda) for clothes – 한복을 입을 거예요 (hanbogeul ibeul geoyeyo). Shoes take 신다 (sinda), hats 쓰다 (sseuda).
때 (ttae = the time of): 휴가 때 (hyuga ttae = during vacation).
Plans are 'built' in Korean: 계획을 세워요 (gyehoegeul sewoyo = make a plan).
랑 (rang) = 'with/and' after a vowel: 친구랑 (chingu-rang = with a friend).
이랑 (irang) = 'and/with' after a consonant: 과일이랑 야채 (gwail-irang yachae); after a vowel it's 랑 (rang).
English says a place is crowded; Korean says the people are many: 사람이 많아요 (saram-i manayo). The crowd is the subject, not the store.
만 오천 (man ocheon) = 15,000 – stack 만 (10,000) and 오천 (5,000).
깎아 주세요 (kkakka juseyo) = 'please lower the price' – normal at markets, but not in fixed-price shops.
좀 (jom) softens statements: 좀 비싸요 (jom bissayo = it's a bit expensive).
중이에요 (jung-ieyo) after a noun = 'in the middle of it': 세일 중이에요 (seil jung-ieyo = it's on sale).
만 (man) after a noun = 'only': 오늘만 (oneul-man = today only) – same sound as the 만 that means 10,000.
Korean has no -er ending – you just put 더 (deo = more) before the word: 더 쌌어요 (deo ssasseoyo) = was cheaper, literally 'more was-cheap'.
쓰다 (sseuda) = write, use, and spend: 돈을 썼어요 (don-eul sseosseoyo = spent money).
Color names usually end in -색 (saek): 파란색 (paransaek = blue).
쓰다 (sseuda) also covers wearing things on your head: 모자를 써요 (moja-reul sseoyo = I wear a hat).
English puts 'new' on the glasses; Korean puts it on the buying: 새로 샀어요 (saero sasseoyo = newly bought).
로 (ro) also marks a role: 선물로 (seonmullo = as a present) – the same ending that covers transport and direction also does 'as'.
Adding 봐요 (bwayo) after a verb = 'try doing it': 입어 봐요 (ibeo bwayo = try it on).
신다 (sinda) = wear on your feet: 신발을 신어요 (sinbal-eul sineoyo = wear shoes).
몇 (myeot) asks 'what number': 몇 사이즈 (myeot saijeu = what size).
한테 (hante) = 'to/for (a person)': 저한테 작아요 (jeohante jagayo = small for me).
조금 (jogeum) = a little; 좀 (jom) is its casual short form.
맞아요 (majayo) spans 'it fits' and 'that's right': 사이즈가 맞아요 (saijeu-ga majayo = the size fits) uses the same word you'd use to agree with someone.
